subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADIAN OVERSEAS TELECOMMUNICATION CORPORATION AND BRITISH POST OFFICE ON CONSTRUCTION OF NEW TRANSATLANTIC CABLE

speakeroldname: Hon. Eric W. Kierans (Minister of Communications):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADIAN OVERSEAS TELECOMMUNICATION CORPORATION AND BRITISH POST OFFICE ON CONSTRUCTION OF NEW TRANSATLANTIC CABLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure to announce to the House the conclusion of an agreement between officials of the Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation and Post Office authorities in the United Kingdom to build a new high capacity transatlantic cable.
The decision to build a new cable, CANTAT-2, is based on projections of a 20 per cent per annum growth in the market for transatlantic circuits during the next 15 years. This is expected to bring the Canadian demand to a level around 4,600 circuits by 1985. A dynamic element in this pattern of growth has been the increase in direct dialing between countries on both sides of the Atlantic.
This bilateral project in which the Canadian investment will be of the order of $37 million will provide 1,840 new telephone circuits on the North Atlantic route between Canada, Britain and Europe. As an indication of the size of this project it should be noted that CANTAT-2 will have 400 more circuits than all existing transatlantic cables, whether they originate in this country or in the United States. Cost of the project will be shared equally by COTC and the British Post Office.
The new high-capacity cable which will link Canada, through a point in Nova Scotia, to Europe at a point in Cornwall is expected to be ready for service early in 1974. This new facility will be added to existing satellite and cable circuits used by COTC to provide reliable and economical telecommunications between Canada and Europe. This project, which has involved months of negotiations between COTC, officials of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Department of
Communications, and their British counterparts, involves several significant advantages for Canada.
Among these numerous advantages are the following. This arrangement provides an alternate commercial route to the transatlantic circuits provided by Intelsat, the international consortium in which COTC is also a shareholder. It provides technological diversity which means greater security for our transatlantic communications links. It provides a system that is compatible with the domestic communications system to be operated by Tele-sat Canada. It assures that Canadian systems will continue to serve as the main route for transpacific Commonwealth traffic. The new cable, therefore, will provide Canadians with more flexibility and reliability in their telecommunications links with Europe.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADIAN OVERSEAS TELECOMMUNICATION CORPORATION AND BRITISH POST OFFICE ON CONSTRUCTION OF NEW TRANSATLANTIC CABLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret the absence of my hon. friend and colleague, the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale), though it gives me satisfaction to comment upon a statement from the Minister of Communications (Mr. Kierans) which bears some of the imprint and impact of being good news. His statement deals with one of the few areas of his extended domain which generally has been successfully operated, namely, the Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation, and to that extent I am very pleased with this new development.
I was interested in a general way to note that the agreement was not made available to us, and obviously this statement is a very general and superficial, and perhaps generous, appraisal of the agreement. One is impressed by the fact that we need more cables, and one is reminded that we have not so completely moved into the era of the satellite as was sometimes predicted in the excitement of a few years ago.
I look forward to receiving further details of this important project. If it allows us to maintain closer contact with other parts of the world in this advancing age of technology, it is something which we welcome. I should like to say that generally I have confidence in the capacity of the COTC to represent Canadian interests in this regard.
I notice that it is intended to integrate, as it must be, this system of cable with the Telesat operation. This is a very important and very costly project which it seems will be much later getting into operation, and at much greater cost, than the minister used to predict. Nevertheless we do feel some satisfaction from the fact that a definite step has been taken in this way to improve our contact with other parts of the world.

From this point of view we are pleased with the announcement.

4.	The survey was based on written questions.
5.	The survey was completed by approximately 17,000 students at 54 universities, community colleges and teachers colleges across Canada. It was based on a scientifically selected sample, within which the response rate averaged 75 per cent.
6.	A full report of the survey including an outline of the method used and a copy of the questionnaire, will be ready in a few weeks time.

Mr. Speaker, I ask leave, seconded by the hon. member for Fraser Valley
Rail Service Negotiations
West (Mr. Rose), to move the adjournment of the House under Standing Order 26 for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely, the interruption of rail service on the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific caused by unwarranted delays in the negotiations between the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers and the railways, the four-month delay before a conciliation board was appointed by the Minister of Labour, the six-month delay before the said board made its report, and the failure of the board to make recommendations on all but two of the more than 20 issues referred to it, and the urgent need to seek an immediate settlement of the dispute in view of the serious effects on the economy of a railway strike affecting the movement of grains, perishables, minerals and other products.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 LABOUR RELATIONS DELAY IN NEGOTIATIONS BETWEEN LOCOMOTIVE ENGINEERS AND RAILWAYS-INTERRUPTION OF RAIL SERVICE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Moose Jaw has given the Chair the notice required under Standing Order 26. Without going into the details of the form of the notice given, I think I should indicate to the hon. member for Moose Jaw that both the notice as given to the Chair and the statement as presented by the hon. member to the House might perhaps be considered as going somewhat beyond the very limited terms of reference allowed to the hon. member by the terms of Standing Order 26, which invites an hon. member to merely state what the matter is that he wishes to be considered by the House. In any event, I can assure the hon. member that I have given the matter very serious consideration.
It is obvious to the House, I am sure, that the hon. member has raised a very important matter which conceivably might require further consideration at some time in the future. After carefully perusing the hon. member's motion, I should like to suggest that the events referred to are in the nature of a developing situation in that the two parties are still, as I understand it, discussing the issue. I do not feel that the Chair can assume that these negotiations are in such a state as to require a debate in the House at the present time under the provisions of Standing Order 26. It should also be observed that if leave were granted to allow a debate under Standing Order 26 at this time, under our rules it would be impossible for the hon. member, or any other hon. member, to raise this issue again during the current session under the terms of Standing Order 26.
Bearing all these considerations in mind, I feel that the motion proposed should not be allowed at this time.

Mr. Chairman, I was interested in the discussion which took place on Friday last and I welcome the opportunity to take part in the debate today, particularly since the subject has to do with the area opened up by my hon. friend from Northumberland-Colchester North, that is to say, the whole question of the realization of the energy potential of the Bay of Fundy in terms of the generation of electricity and other economic advantages.

The Bay of Fundy tidal program review board, following its most recent assessment, concluded that it would not be economical to go ahead with such a project now, and I have dealt with that aspect. Without impugning the integrity of this board at all, its engineering and economic models were based on information that was outdated. Its methods of construction were outdated, and its costing was outdated. The fact is that interest rates today are lower than they were. The fact is that new and more efficient methods have been developed. Indeed, it is now commonly conceded that a sustained source of power could be developed on an economic basis.
I say it is inevitable that the Bay of Fundy tides will be harnessed. It is inevitable if for no other reason than that it is the cheapest source of power we can find. It is a renewable resource which provides power. Most important of all, it is pollution free. I suggest to the minister that we must approach the development of these tides openly and with frankness. And if we do fumble the ball, it will be many, many years before we will be able to pick it up again, because in the interval we will become deeply involved in programs of uranium enrichment and automatic self-breeders. I do not want atomic waste buried in my backyard, not when there is available pure, clean water which prevents no danger or pollution hazard. If we fumble the ball again, then these are the problems with which we will be confronted with respect to developing the Bay of Fundy tides. Mr. Chairman, that, I thought, was the arrangement. I was not aware that hon. members opposite had finished so promptly, and that is why I did not get up. I will be very pleased to make such a statement, and to answer such questions as have been asked in committee to the best of my ability.
First, Mr. Speaker, may I point out that the bill itself, and I think some hon. members were concerned about this, does not give any new powers to the department. I believe the hon. member for Kamouraska, in particular, asked why hydroelectric energy was included in the bill, and whether the words in paragraph (a) of clause 8 "energy, including energy developed from water," had any particular significance. I believe other hon. members also asked why mines and other non-renewable resources were included, and whether that part constituted new powers. I think it might be useful if, at the outset, I tried to clarify that point. May I emphasize that no new powers are envisaged with respect to energy, mines, resources and technical surveys in the bill as it is constituted.
The purpose of clause 8 is to clarify the relative responsibilities of the new department which is acquiring the water expertise that was formerly in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources and what is left in the continuing Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. The problem is that, although formerly most of the water expertise within the government was included in the department and now most of that expertise is going to the new department, the words "including energy development from water" are included in subclause (a) of clause 8 in order to indicate that while water generally is going to the new department in its aspect vis-a-vis the development of hydroelectric power, that particular expertise will remain within the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. That is the reason those words are included there. When it refers to mines, minerals and other non-renewable resources, again this does not connote a new power to the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources but is merely indicative of the fact that the basic line of demarcation between the new department and the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources will be that distinction between renewable as opposed to non-renewable resources.
The renewable resources generally will be in the new department of the environment, if this House sees fit to pass the bill. The non-renewable resources generally will be continued in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. While I say there will be no new powers, and that that is not the purpose of clause 8, I think it is inherent within the division of powers as envisaged by the demarcation between renewable and non-renewable resources that the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources will be more inclined than it has been in the past to be an economics department. I think hon. members here have indicated some concern that there is not
[The Chairman.]
March 29, 1971

sufficient economic forethought, if you like, given to the planning of the use of our resources and energy resources in particular. That may well be a valid criticism of the past. I think the emphasis in the past with regard to the development of our mineral resources, our energy resources and our non-renewable resources generally, was to develop them and to find markets for them. I believe that until fairly recently that was pretty well what we were concerned with; that is, the economic growth, if you like, as applied to these resources as well as others.
I think it is very clear, not merely from the well understood indications that were shown in the debate here but from the debate generally in the country and in the world, that the importance of resources, and mineral resources in particular as well as non-renewable resources generally in the future, may be much greater than we had appreciated in the past. The equation may be put as simply as this. In a world that will double in population in the next 30 or 35 years, as the prognosticators indicate, in a world in which it took from the beginning of time to put some 3.5 billion people on earth, we will put that many more people on earth in perhaps 30 or 35 years. The population of the world expects what we have deemed to be a high standard of living. Even in the third world, the undeveloped world where the standard of living is so deplorable, the people, I believe probably more than others, want their standard of living to grow and expand. That inevitably means that the finite resources, energy and mineral, will be that much more important and valuable.
Under such circumstances I believe it is quite clear that possibly there needs to be a new emphasis in a country such as Canada, which is so rich in these resources, on the economic planning of the use of these resources, first for domestic purposes because Canadian interests must be paramount, and secondly for use in respect of Canada's position in the world in the years ahead. So, certainly there will be this new emphasis in a department whose main function to date has been the encouragement of development rather than economic planning in respect of the use of the resources. I think probably the old department of mines and technical surveys exemplified the philosophy that lay behind our energy and resource development people when they provided the infrastructure, if you like, scientific and technological, for development. The scientific services were there. The geological surveys were made and that information was available to the world at large. We said, here is the information with which you can look for minerals in the most likely areas. That was probably the main, if not the sole, function of the department.
Certainly, while I say there are no new powers envisaged within the bill, I cannot deny the connotations in the speeches of so many members that a new emphasis is required. I believe this is clearly understood, even though no new specific powers are envisaged in the bill. I think the demarcation in respect of emphasis on environment and renewable resources in one department, as opposed to the emphasis on non-renewable resources in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, clearly
Government Organization Act, 1970 indicates that the government appreciates that these two are affected in some way parallel in this country and in the kind of world in which we find ourselves today.
I do not believe I can today answer all the very valid questions asked by many members during the course of the debate so far, but I shall do my best at least to give a general review of what has taken place to date. First, I think the main concern has been in respect of energy policies rather than mineral policies, if I understood the tenor of the debate. At the outset, I may say there is no such thing as a static and continuing or constant energy policy. I do not think I could ever, no matter how effective and complete our research and planning should be, stand up in this House and say that here is the energy policy for Canada. We should then forget about it, because it is there for the next few years and we could turn our attention in this House to something else. Energy policy does not lend itself to that kind of definitive, lasting solution.
I might illustrate this best in this way. Let us say we attempted to have this sort of a complete and comprehensive over-all policy and then next week, as might well be the case, a new situation should arise. Suppose the rumour was proven true that there had been a great find of oil on the east coast, and we announced an over-all energy policy that did not take such a find into consideration. Quite obviously, we would have to rush out and revise our energy policy. That is why I say that the energy policy generally is fluid and changing, and must be so if we are to use our energy resources and meet the demands in the best interests of the total economy. In our thinking on the energy policy and where the policies of the government must go if we are to have the most effective direction in the national interest, I think it is most useful-and this is the way we have taken in the department and with the agencies that report to me-to think rather of policy objectives. What are the objectives of the use of energy in Canada? In this regard, we can classify some of those objectives.
The economic objective is one of them, to make the best economic use of our resources. National security is very clearly one of the objectives of our energy policy, because no modern industrial state such as Canada can be founded on anything but the most secure sources of supply that it can achieve, bearing in mind that these objectives have to be related one to the other. We would not want complete security at the price of economic foolhardiness. If we had complete security at too high a price for energy that the consumers of Canada, both industrial and household, paid, then we would have paid too high a price for security. Again these varying objectives have to be related.
Another objective is resource adequacy. That is certainly one of the great problems. As I said at the beginning of my remarks, assuring the adequacy of our resources has been, until fairly recently, our paramount objective. The quality of the environment is a fairly new objective. Until a very few years ago most of us did not foresee-and I certainly was not among the wise who

March 29, 1971
Government Organization Act, 1970 knew 10, 15 or 20 years ago-that this would be one of the paramount objectives in 1971; yet today it is clearly so.
If there is one criticism I have to make with respect to the debate, it is that there is an inclination to think, perhaps naturally, that the federal Parliament can solve these major problems without considering jurisdictional problems. However, under our constitution, the ownership of the energy resources is very clearly vested in the provinces. While we can say, yes, we have control of exports and hence we have a lever, which is extremely important and powerful, I think, as with many of the delicate balances within our constitution, we must attempt to consider jurisdictional problems which quite often are interlaced with economic problems. Certainly, so far as oil and gas are concerned, at the present time there is an inclination on the part of the province of Alberta to be rather more concerned with achieving the maximum returns from the product since most of these products now are situated in that province. The maximum return to Alberta, can be achieved through royalties resulting from the most rapid exploitation and development of these resources. On the other hand, I feel sure that to foist a completely unrealistic price upon the eastern Canadian consumers in order to achieve a maximum exploitation of resources in the west, particularly in Alberta where the resources are found, would be an untoward balance jurisdictionally in economic terms visa-vis the producers as opposed to the consumers.
Undoubtedly, this has been the story of Canada in so many of our economic endeavours. We have tried to achieve a balance jurisdictionally among the interests of the various sectors of Canada, bearing in mind that under our constitution the resources themselves are under the immediate jurisdictional authority of the provinces. Sometimes it is forgotten that the producing provinces of today may not be the major producing provinces of tomorrow. I often think that if we had designed policies for the objective of maximizing the well-being of the producing provinces at the expense of the consumer provinces, they would help one province today. However, the greatest potential for development of oil, gas and petroleum products in general outside federal territories is to be found in the provinces that are not the producers of today.
The Gulf of St. Lawrence is a great potential area, and so is the Atlantic and the offshore areas. Achieving that balance between consumer and producer interests will serve in the long run the very provinces which today feel they are not so well served by the policies because they tend one way or the other.
Public revenue is certainly one of the objectives which we must consider at all times. I do not think it would be acceptable to leave all of the returns from our natural resources, from our energy resources in particular, in the hands of entrepreneurs and developers. On the other hand, if we load too heavily those resources with what is known in the trade as "front-end loadings", either in provincial areas by provincial rules or in federal lands by federal taxes under our own rules and regulations, which would push up the price of the product, we might
well put some of that product out of the economic stream. This is particularly opposite in the northern territories where gas and oil would become very expensive. We were finding that out when we discussed in the House and elsewhere the problems of transporting oil and gas from the northern territories. We know how costly that may be.
There is a factor which would be of interest to members of the House, one which I came across the other day. In the Ontario market, 88 per cent of the cost of natural gas is the cost of transportation, and only 12 per cent is the wellhead cost of that gas. So, in the case of northern oil and gas, transportation costs will be an even more important factor. The costs of transportation are so great that if we front-end load the product with too heavy a cost, we will possibly price it out of the market for many years to come.
Our policy, as contrasted with that of the state of Alaska, would be interesting to hon. members in considering the problem. As hon. members know, the problems in the province of Alaska-the state of Alaska, it is not yet a province, I do not think-

don't front-end load the costs. The time to get the money is when markets are found and the resources are flowing. The way to get revenue is from royalties. The decision as to whether the markets will be domestic or foreign is one that will be made by the government, the Parliament of that day. So, I think we can see the diametrically opposed policies of Alaska and Canada, and in our respectful view the Canadian position is superior in that we are not pricing ourselves out of markets ahead of time. We are not putting an undue burden on the domestic economy. We are keeping our options open. It has been said that the Maritime provinces are among the have-not provinces. That may be so in economic terms, but I have never found that they are among the have-nots in terms of the quality of life that exists in that part of Canada. But certainly from the standpoint of

economics, I can think of nothing that would solve the economic problems of the Maritime provinces more than substantial and economic petroleum finds in the off-shore. I think that many of us of my vintage remember when Alberta was a have-not province. Certainly, it was the discovery of the very rich petroleum resources there that converted that province from a have-not into one of the really "have" provinces.
So again, if it is a social objective to give greater economic opportunity in the so-called have-not regions, then policies tending to encourage the exploration of those areas, whereby petroleum reserves may be found, are the kind of policies we must have in order to attain that objective. In the brief time at my disposal I am not really able to go over each of those particular objectives, and how government policies attempt to gear themselves to achieve those objectives, and to achieve a balance between those objectives in the total national interest. I think, however, I could briefly go over the economic objectives and indicate something on this subject to the House, because I believe most of the debate so far has been in respect of economic objectives. I think most of the criticism, or the doubt as to the validity of government policies, was centred in this area of economic objectives.
First, one of our chief economic objectives is to achieve the lowest cost energy mix so far as may be consistent with recovery of social cost and social objectives which involve a price tax penalty on uses of energy. Second, our objective is to realize the maximum over-all benefits to Canada from the domestic energy industries through making available a variety of energy supplies and facilitating the export of surplus energy at optimum prices. In other words, we think one of the fundamentals of Canada's energy policy, which may not have been appreciated, is to give the consumer, be he an industrial consumer or household consumer, the greatest possible mix of competing energy resources, and I mean truly competing.
I think we have seen this. I think it was not too long ago that there were many areas where the household consumer had two choices for heating his home, coal or oil. In most of those communities today he has four choices, coal, oil, hydro electricity, and natural gas. As I say, we have felt the policy should be to give this kind of true competition between energy resources themselves and in this method, by real competition, we would achieve the lowest cost and the greatest maximum choice for the consumer. In this regard, and despite some opinions expressed to the contrary, I do not think we can ever isolate the Canadian consumer from generally rising global energy costs. There is no way I know of that we can say, "Energy costs in the world are going up, but in some way we can keep them down for Canadian consumers despite world economic trends." I do not think this can be done. We do live in the world. We market our products in the world.
If we try to do this, attractive although it might appear, in our view what would happen would be that we would not get the kind of exploration, research and development in Canada's energy industries that would in fact keep costs down, no matter how great our supplies
Government Organization Act, 1970 may be, or how great our potential may be. One thing that has been made manifest in the last year or two is that risk capital available for exploration and development in the petroleum game is global capital. There is no such thing as domestic capital for exploration. It moves throughout the world to where the prospects are likeliest, and it is a finite amount.
No matter how powerful are the corporate entities, incidentally some of them owned by governments with all the financial power of governments behind them, and no matter how powerful are the great private corporations, they do not have unlimited amounts of money for exploration, particularly for frontier exploration. They go to where the prospects are best. We have seen this happen. We have seen a great movement into the North Sea where there was very little exploration activity until a few years ago, at which time there was a find. We have seen a great movement to the eastern off-shore in Canada because the geological prospects were good. Incidentally, and with humility, I think the geographical survey of Canada, and those responsible for it deserve a great deal of the credit for having done the spade work which demonstrated the geological interest of the off-shore, both on the east coast and in the north.
Certainly, Mr. Chairman, these corporations go where the geology is good. They go where the political climate is good. Certainly, they will not be so prone to go to a country where, if they find oil, they may be expropriated the next week. And they go where they can market the product at a good return if they are successful in their exploratory activities. If we fix prices inordinately low in Canada, it appears to us all that this would result in the biggest proportion of the exploratory dollar going someplace else. Because if world prices are at a certain level, and Canadian prices are far below that, it must be remembered that it costs just as much to find oil here, and one of the principal costs of oil is that involved in finding it. I thank hon. members for granting me this indulgence.
So, Mr. Chairman, I say our policies are not founded on the premise that because we have this great potential in Canada-I think the best estimates are that as yet only 10 per cent of our petroleum resources have been uncovered-therefore energy resources should be very cheap in this country. They will not be uncovered, even though they exist, if we think we can shelter from world conditions. I do think that we can have advantageous

March 29, 1971
Government Organization Act, 1970
prices as compared with countries with no natural resources, but they must be related. If the price of energy increases throughout the world, so must the Canadian price. Although we must ensure that our prices do not increase as rapidly as others, still we cannot shelter completely or we will not get the development.
An example of this is the problem being faced by the United States at the present time with regard to natural gas. Contrary to opinion which has not researched the facts carefully, there is no innate shortage of natural gas in the United States at the present time. There is, however, a shortage of proven resources of natural gas. The opinions of the best experts that I have been able to read on this subject attribute this to the fact that prices were set too low perhaps because there was considerable political input. If the assessments that appear to be most valid are correct, it would appear that a few years ago the price of natural gas in the United States was so low it did not pay the entrepreneur to go and look for it. He took his money to other places in the world or invested it in bonds or something else, because looking for natural gas did not bring a good return on investment. The proof of the pudding in this regard is that today, when there is a problem of supply in proven resources of natural gas in the United States,-they have a great potential for producing gas from coal

regulatory agencies are revising the prices under contracts for natural gas in order to encourage more development and to ensure a good return to investors. They know that only by this method can they uncover more resources and meet the problems of shortage of supply in the future. Just because we have the potential in Canada, we cannot expect to shelter from the rising energy costs of the world. We can only make sure that we are always in a competitive or preferred position.
The third of the economic objectives of the policy directions for the development of over-all energy policies which will result in optimum economic efficiencies in all sectors of the energy industry, ranging from primary production to ultimate consumption must take into account such factors as the rates at which Canadian energy resources should be developed relative to Canadian energy needs and export possibilities; application of appropriate principles of conservation based upon developing technology, including such factors as increased recovery; minimization of waste; efficiency of energy conversion; utilization of by-products; substitution of more abundant energy sources in places of scarce energy sources; proper utilization of all energy sources, including imports within the consuming sector based upon cost-price relationships; premium quality of certain energy sources; appropriate contribution of each source to public revenue; pollution control aspects; consumer preference and convenience; the appropriate form and extent of government intervention which would range from exhortation through to state ownership within each sector of the energy industry and for each source of energy; the impact of other policies of government on energy matters; the integration of energy policies with other policies in order that energy development may make a major contribution toward national and regional goals. These
economic objectives call for the selection of policies relative to the availability and use of an expanding economic supply of energy which are based on analysis of cost-price relationships, energy industry performance under the various market and price circumstances, and the proper role of government.
These, Mr. Chairman, are generally the concepts with which the government attempts to approach the very difficult question of energy policies in Canada. To date, most of the production is in one region and most of the consumption is in another. As is so often the case in the Canadian conundrum, over the years decisions have probably been made which are not purely economic decisions-just as the CPR decision might not have been the best economic one at the time of confederation, though it made confederation possible. The decision regarding the original Trans-Canada pipeline was of that nature. Unquestionably, the natural economic market for Alberta gas was the midwest of the United States. As hon. members will recall, some people thought that Alberta gas should be shipped to its natural economic market of the midwest and the eastern markets of eastern Canada should be served with gas from the United States in exchange. That proposal was not accepted. The tradition and the necessity was to have transportation lines going east and west, and this included railway lines as well as natural gas pipelines. We found the typical Canadian solution and said that the major concern must be Canadian markets for Canadian natural gas. The Trans-Canada line was built, but in order to make the exploration and production economically viable, the surplus was set aside for the export market. Had it not been so, the entire exercise might not have been possible.
It is along these lines, Mr. Chairman, that hon. members have raised the very valid and possibly pregnant question of Canada's national oil policy which I think has been in existence since 1961. Whatever may be the current problems or the current need for review, I do not doubt that the time has come for us to take a very careful look at our oil policy. Whatever may be its present needs I think we can be happy with the past results. Whatever the need for the future, the policy has worked very well up to now, and I wish all our economic policies were as successful as the national oil policy and the national energy policy.
One of our great prime ministers, upon returning from a trip abroad and hearing some complaints from the opposition said, "I am surprised when I get back to hear how bad things are in Canada because I can assure you in many other parts of the world that I visited I found they would gladly exchange their problems for ours." I think that view would be a valid one with regard to Canada's oil and energy policies. Many things have contributed to the success of our oil policy. This success was partly, the result of policy, partly good timing in the world at large, partly good management by those responsible for managing, by the people in industry. Whatever the reason, the policies have worked well.
Our reserves of crude oil and natural gas liquids were 5.6 million barrels in 1963 and 10.4 million barrels in

March 29, 1971

1970. During that period, our reserves have just about doubled. These reserves can be used for whatever purpose we see fit from time to time. If in 1970 the Canadian government decided it was not going to export any more, it could do that. It would then be in the position of having almost double the reserves of seven years ago. Certainly, we would be in a far better position because of the policies which existed up to this point, including the policy of export which has enabled that kind of reserve.
I now wish to deal with the volume of sales during that period. The value of total sales in 1963 was $682 million. In 1970, it was $1,250 million. That not only connotes revenues to the federal government, and very great revenues in the form of royalties to the provincial governments, but a great deal of employment. This employment aspect includes people in the field doing the exploratory work and people in the factories of eastern Canada, including the province of Quebec. All our research indicates that the multiplier effect of the resource industries is very great. Also included are the people who produce the drilling equipment, rigs, steel and so on. These figures do not represent mere cash or profit. The sales figures represent a great deal of employment and economic well-being in Canada.
During the same period, our exports of Canadian oil also increased. The figure for 1963 is 260,000 barrels and for 1970, 750,000 barrels per day. Domestic sales of 520,000 barrels per day in 1963 increased to 700,000 barrels per day in 1970. Canada's net self-sufficiency in oil has increased from about 77 per cent in 1963 to about 100 per cent in 1970. I suggest that is an extremely important statistic.
With regard to our policies of expanding our export markets and maximizing our sales, the government is doing its best to improve the markets for those who have found oil. We are trying to get this oil to the market which pays the best price in the world, namely the United States market which is highly protected by the U.S. government. We could not compete if this market were wide open. The countries of the Far East could sell their oil much more cheaply than Canada. We have achieved a considerable inroad into the United States market. That kind of market place, as well as the Canadian domestic place, has encouraged exploration in Canada. It costs a great deal of money to keep a barrel of oil in inventory, just as it does to keep any item in inventory for an untoward period of time. If the market place is not available, we will not engender the kind of exploration which will give us the maximum development of our petroleum resources.
The fact is that these policies have worked and have engendered a great deal of exploration during the period 1963-70. Canada has gone from a deficit position where it was dependent on offshore oil, a position of some difficulty, to the position of being a self-sufficient nation. Today, Canada is 100 per cent self sufficient in oil, we deem that that is what we want to be.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know if I have those specific figures. If my memory serves me right, 1 believe that approximately one half of our oil consumption is from offshore purchases. I want to be fair to the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands. With regard to the question of security, he feels that we should seriously consider the question of whether we should build a pipeline to Montreal, thereby making us more secure. I agree that this would provide a greater security. A greater percentage of our total country could then be directly served by Canadian oil. The question is whether this would be a good policy at the present time.
When I say that approximately one half of our needs are met by offshore oil, this means that we are conserving or replacing the resources that we use. The hon. member takes the opposite view with regard to natural gas. If I understand his argument correctly, his view is that we should conserve because this natural gas will be needed further downstream. He feels that we should conserve, rather than export. With respect, I do not think he can have his argument both ways. If that is valid vis-a-vis natural gas, then that is exactly what happens with respect to oil. We are now replacing the oil which we use by importing offshore oil at a far cheaper price than that at which we sell. If we can replace non-renewable resources with imports of offshore oil at a lower price, that is a pretty good policy. In fact, it is sometimes too good a policy. Our friends to the south, particularly those in the New England states, would like to be able to do exactly what we are doing. The policy of conservation possibly could not be justified if it stultified the growth of our own natural gas industry, the petroleum industry in particular. Such is not the case. As I indicated, that industry has been particularly healthy during the period when these policies have worked.

As I understand it, the Borden commission concluded that a pipeline to the Montreal market would not be sound economics for Canada. We should achieve an admixture, which is the Canadian tradition in many areas, with major movement east and west. The Ontario market would be reserved for western oil. Exports to the south render the whole exercise viable in economic terms.
What we could have done, and I suppose what we could still do, though I suggest the argument for so doing is becoming even less convincing than it was during the

This must surely have resulted in one of two things. The cost of the pipeline would have to be underwritten in the cost of the oil; we could have kept wellhead prices low so as to keep prices relatively low in the east market, or we could have asked the eastern consumers to pay a far higher price for then-gasoline and petroleum products. With respect, I think this would have amounted to a misuse of our resources. In my view we have had the best of all worlds. We have earned a considerable amount of foreign currency, which is badly needed, and we have been able to keep consumer prices down in the eastern market while at the same time enabling the western producer in a large measure to get optimum prices for his production.
I must admit that the national oil policy, when you look at it as such, is a strange-looking bird-the Ottawa Valley line, and so on, part of Canada being served by offshore oil and another part of Canada by domestic oil. This pol'cy does not possess the completeness, the rational perfection which the academician so admires. But it works. It works well. It has resulted in a healthy oil industry. It has made possible the best possible prices in eastern Canada, taking supplies which are the most competitive on world markets. At the same time, it has enabled us to earn a considerable amount in foreign currency. Maybe this arrangement will not work forever. This is one of the problems regarding opening up the United States market further to our production, if that is deemed to be in our interest, that we do already in fact have the best of all worlds.

Perhaps I might answer one of hon. members' questions. Some hon. members keep asking me for a specific review, a specific feasibility study. My best information is that from the time of the Borden report, the National Energy Board, which certainly has considerable expertise in this area, has kept under constant and continuous review world prices, construction costs, cost of right of way and so on. It is the opinion of my officials, including officials of the Board, that while the economics are closer than at the time of the Borden Commission Report, the situation is not such that at the present time it would be a valid enterprise unless wellhead costs were reduced in the west, or consumer prices were increased in the east. While the equation is getting more favourable I suggest with respect it would be premature, until we know one way or another in the next two or three years what is going to happen in connection with the exploration programs in the north and offshore, to embark on the construction of a Montreal pipeline.
I do not know how long hon. members are going to be patient with me. I should like to mention the subject of the northern pipeline which was raised in most of the speeches made so far by hon. members in this portion of the debate. Hon. members were very properly interested in determining exactly what, if anything, had been done by the government in preparation for such a northern pipeline. May I say at the outset that I believe there is a misconception as to the basis of the government's research. We have never approached the research from the standpoint of it being up to the government to determine how, when and under what terms a pipeline should be built.
As I understand our law, and the National Energy Board Act in particular, what we must prepare ourselves to do is to assess properly and effectively any application for construction so that we can make a decision in the interests of the Canadian public generally both present and future. This has an important connotation. It means that a great deal of the research is done not at the expense of the taxpayers of Canada but, very properly, at the expense of those who may gain economic benefits as a legitimate result of their research, as builders of pipelines and entrepreneurs. If the government did all of

the research and then decided when and how the pipeline was to be built, this would tremendously increase the cost to the Canadian taxpayers, and I do not think would be in keeping with our present law. It may be that Parliament, sometime later, will decide that it is up to government to build pipelines or to determine how and when pipelines should be built and that all research into the question should be conducted at public expense.
Our approach, and we believe it is sound, has been to prepare ourselves to deal with questions of economics, ecology, pipeline construction, safety of the tundra, the problem of permafrost and so on, so that if an application is made we can enlarge upon the guidelines of last August which resulted from the government's preliminary investigations over a period of two years. I think hon. members are more than familiar with them. What we said, in effect, was that these were the general guidelines to which any entrepreneur can look if he wishes to build a pipeline. As our research becomes more complete, I think undoubtedly we should define them more precisely and make the rules more clear and specific.
With regard to the wellbeing of indigenous peoples, the routing of the pipeline falls under the responsibility of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development whose department, as I understand it, acts as a province would jurisdictionally in provincial areas. Undoubtedly, further clarification here is required. But may I emphasize to hon. members that our research has been oriented toward preparing all government agencies to deal effectively and responsibly, in the interests of the Canadian public, with any pipeline application that may be made.
We have not conducted our research as though we were going to go ahead and build the pipeline. We did feel that a considerable proportion of the cost should be borne by the public sector, and it has been; but a very major proportion should be borne by those who are economically interested in the potential of a pipeline, those who may reap reward from its construction. In all fairness their research has been made known to us. We have been kept abreast of everything they have been doing and have been permitted to share in their knowledge. Indeed, we have joined them in their research whenever we have wished.
I think it is of interest to note that from the standpoint of actual construction, it may be that a more comprehensive day to day type of research has been conducted by those entrepreneurs who contemplated building the Valdez line in Alaska. If they turn their attention to the possibility of a Mackenzie valley route, then we will, of course, expect them to make all their knowledge and information available to the Canadian government and its agencies in our determination of whether or not such a Mackenzie Valley route would be in the interest of the public of Canada. So again, in that sense, we are attempting to get the best of both worlds by obtaining information from both private and public sectors.

The minister has had a long spell and may be getting a little tired. While he is on this subject and his mind is fresh, may I ask him a question or two about pipelines.
The minister says that the government's position, in the main, is that it will respond to an application rather than do the preliminary work itself. It seems to me there are really three matters that have to be dealt with when any application to build a pipeline is made. These are, the effect of the line on the ecology, conducting an economic feasibility study, and what I would call the Canadian ownership or control aspect.
With respect to the ecology, I noticed that the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry said the other day in a speech he made in Vancouver that at the present time only the engineering and economic aspects are being discussed. There is relatively very little ecological data available to the National Energy Board. Under those circumstances, on what will the National Energy Board make this decision regarding the ecological effects? Are they going to accept the report of the company? We have all had pretty bad experiences in days gone by of governments accepting the opinions of interested parties as to what will be the result of a certain project.
As members of Parliament, we are going to become acquainted with such a project only after the National Energy Board has recommended it and the government has endorsed the proposal. Therefore, it is of some concern to us to know on what ecological studies will the National Energy Board and government base their decisions. Will a decision be made on the basis of the company's studies? Will studies be made of the effects of such a line on wildlife, on permafrost, on the tundra? It seems to me we need clarification of that point.
With regard to the economic feasibility study, I agree that the National Energy Board is competent to deal with that aspect.
The other matter on which I wish to say a word is what I call the Canadian ownership and control aspect. If a pipeline is to be build from Alaska through Canada to the United States, under the guidelines it has to be a common carrier. But what does that mean? It can be a common carrier only if we have something to say about the input and output. The only advantage to Canada of such a pipeline-apart from what little employment we may receive from the original construction of the line- would be that Canada could put oil into the pipeline. But is this oil that is going mainly to the United States? Is it oil that is going to increase our exports to the United States, or is it going to be piped into Canada for shipment to eastern Canada to meet the increased needs of Canadian consumers?
If this is to be the case then who is going to own and control the pipeline? If the line is going to be entirely U.S. owned, is the United States going to decide the flow?

Before the government embarks upon discussions, does it have in mind reserving a certain part of the capacity of the line for Canadian input and output? Who is going to set the rates? If the rates are set abnormally high, then the fact that it is a common carrier becomes meaningless.
It seems to me we should ask the minister these questions since we shall get very little chance to ask them after the deal is signed, sealed and delivered. I cannot believe that the government is discussing with the oilmen only a land bridge through Canada rather than the TAPS route-which in our opinion would be a disaster. But if it is talking about a land route, surely the government must have given some thought, first to the ecology question, and second to how ownership and control of the line would be exercised, and what protection Canadians would have with respect thereto.

May I say what we are attempting to do. We realize that this would not be a normal type of application. Normally, the National Energy Board Act governs. We know that the National Energy Board employs engineers, economists and scientists with a great deal of expertise, and we, as a government, do not usually involve ourselves in applications for the building of pipelines, except to ratify a decision or to dissent from a recommendation. But this, obviously, is of such economic and social moment that it is important from the point of view of Canada that the government should involve itself in a way it does not normally in respect of ordinary pipeline applications.
The hon. member has asked whether we will take at face value the ecological studies of the oil companies. We certainly will not take their studies alone at face value. The Minister of Fisheries and Forestry has already said in a speech, I believe, that such studies are not sufficiently ecologically downstream, so to speak, and that may be so. He was speaking of the ecology. He said that he has a particular interest in the wildlife studies. Certainly, those studies are not the responsibility of my department, and we have not done very much about the wildlife situation. I believe that the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, under the ALURA program, supports studies of this sort. I think that perhaps the new minister who will have responsibilities in this field will want to go ahead with such studies.
While talking of ecological studies generally may I say that the interdepartmental task force on northern oil as I indicated in my last review before the House, has appointed four subcommittees. One of those subcommittees was specifically the subcommittee to study ecological problems. My information is that that subcommittee is now sufficiently advanced in its work and will either issue or give to the government-perhaps I should not make them public because I do not know what the gov-

ernment will intend to do here-its guidelines. It seems to me that when we get their report we will look back to our own general, public guidelines and we will see that we said that one of the factors to be considered is the protection of the ecology. We will receive this report and we will be able, therefore, to enlarge upon it and say, "the ecology now means a, b, c, d, and e." I hope this research will go that far and, hence, that the picture will be made clearer in advance of an application being made.
Of course, both the departments as well as other departments, and the National Energy Board will be taking advantage of the research of the industry. I hope that we are able to assist them actively. Nevertheless, and I could not agree more with the hon. member in this, we must not overlook the fact, and I do not think anyone in this House overlooks it, that the oil industry, historically, not in Canada but globally, has not been altruistic and beneficent in its attitude to the public but has been, rather, a highly profit motivated industry. I could not agree more with the hon. member in that assertion. Certainly, we must look at these studies objectively.
For instance, I note that one of the companies is undertaking a study of the migration of caribou, a subject which I think the hon. member for Athabasca raised in one of his questions. We must consider this problem. Will the caribou cross the pipeline, or will the pipeline affect their migration, and, thus, not only the well-being of the wildlife of the area but the ability of the indigenous people who live off the caribou to maintain themselves. I am sure that we will not take the industry's study of the migration of the caribou at face value. The wildlife services will investigate the matter for themselves. I hope, thus, that we can make objective judgments and translate these into guidelines wherever possible or give the pertinent information to the National Energy Board, for it to consider in hearing applications.
The hon. member also asked about the regulatory authority over the line. May I point out to him that one of the guidelines in this area specifically says that the National Energy Board Act will prevail and that this pipeline, wherever it is built, if it cuts across Canada will come under the jurisdiction of the National Energy Board. That fact clearly indicates and connotes that it will be under Canadian regulatory authority.
The government could not agree more with another observation of the hon. member. If our land is used merely as a land bridge to enable American resources to get to American market places I would be the first to say, "go somewhere else." I would hate to see the oil pipeline go into Valdez, and then have the oil taken by tanker. But if that is all we were, a land bridge, I do not think we could consider a pipeline at all across the Mackenzie and I think our guidelines make this very clear. Nevertheless, in this area we cannot be specific or definitive, yet. We cannot say exactly what we mean by "common carrier" with respect to the pipeline. Because of the economics of the pipeline we do not know, yet, just how economic a proposition this is going to be and how much we can transgress on normal rules of economics and still have the line. If it turns out that this line can only be
March 29, 1971

built in such a way that Canadians can only enter this line it there is slack in it, then we can say that we do not want the line under those conditions. However, we do not want to make a pre-judgment until all the economic tacts are available.
There are problems connected, of course, with the economic concept. This is to be a very, very long line. If you fill the line completely with oil all the way from Prudhoe Bay to the United States, you will get a 100 per cent use of that line. If three quarters of the way to the market place a Canadian company wishes to introduce Canadian oil into the line and we say, "stop, you must make room for the Canadian oil in the line", then, of course, you will introduce slack in the line all the way back to Prudhoe Bay, or in about three quarters of the line, which might be an uneconomic or unprofitable use of the line or a "non-use" of the line.
As I understand it, under the present rules with respect to lines governed by the National Energy Board, the common carrier concept applies to oil lines presently, and not to gas lines. The board's concept works this way: if a downstream or downline user, in the judgment of the board, has an economic supply-some fellow with a thimble full of oil cannot come along and upset the economics of the line-it is up to the pipeline operators to allow this fellow to transport his oil. That is their responsibility, and that is one of the conditions of the original certificate. Whether this concept would work in this instance, and whether this would be a valid approach to the Mackenzie Valley line, we do not know yet.
May I say this with great respect to the House and to the country generally which is concerned about these problems, and quite properly so. Until a clearer picture of the economics of the line is seen, we really will not be able to tell how many burdens, if you like, which might be very much in the Canadian interest we can place on this line. Some of these decisions must await, therefore, the event of the application.
If, on the application, we see that this line cannot be a common carrier and that there is no way in which we can force Canadian oil into the line, our course is clear. Our guidelines clearly say that under those terms we must say, "we are sorry, but you cannot build the pipeline." Nevertheless, I feel certain from discussions to date, and from conversations I have had, that there will be an accommodation for Canadian oil in that line, and there must be such accommodation. We can determine these matters when an application is made. If the companies say, "if you want any more than that, you boys will be right out of the ball game," we can then decide to say, "it is you who are out of the ball game." Nevertheless, I do not think we should slam the door until, at least, we get a look at the horse. We should not close the barn door before we see the horse, if I may use such an analogy in my present non-agricultural portfolio.

I will see if I can find the exact wording. I may be paraphrasing, but I believe the wording is to the effect that there will be "substantial opportunity to Canadians for participating in the financing, engineering, construction, ownership and management of the pipeline." Now again, the wording "substantial opportunity" is not very definitive. Members may find it is not very helpful. From all the economic advice we could obtain at the time, whatever may have been our shortcomings, we knew we did not know very much about the economics. That may not be to our very great credit, but obviously neither did anybody else. I believe it is becoming more and more manifest that this undertaking is of such gigantic proportion that in terms of Canadian experience it is almost beyond anything that has ever happened to us. Although I do not know the exact answer, I have heard figures kicked around running all the way from $4 billion to $8 billion for the two lines, and with all the good will in the world I cannot help the House concerning which figures are accurate. I doubt whether anyone else can.
It is thus quite obvious it would be impossible to raise in Canada a very substantial proportion of the amount of money required. When one takes a look at our total economy and the total amount of Canadian savings in a year, it does not look likely. The ideal, if we could do so, would be to find a Canadian entrepreneur who would ensure that the equity would be in Canada and the debt would be somewhere else. That is the way Trans-Canada was financed. I think we would all be happy with such a situation. This, however, may not be possible. From my discussions with representatives of the companies, as well as the other research entities, I am quite certain that in respect of the engineering, construction and management we will have no problem in having maximum Canadian content. I think this will be so because I believe we are as good as anybody else in the world in this particular field. I am not worried about materials. I think every Canadian pipe manufacturing company and every Canadian steel manufacturing company would be engaged for four or five years if these lines were built. I am informed that with regard to the construction of 48 inch or larger pipe, every entity in the world which manufactures such pipe would be going full tilt.

Government Organization Act, 1970
On the matter of financing, as I said we want the maximum Canadian content and, other things being equal, whoever comes up with the maximum Canadian content will be the winner. However, it is quite possible there will not be more than one application. As I say, it will take all the resources of all the companies put together to even have a hope. So, we have particularly let them know our concern about Canadian content but have not frozen out anything. We will give Canadians all the opportunity they want, but if they do not pick it up there might be an offer which would mean the control would be in non-Canadian hands and we might or might not accept that. It is a matter of having a look before we would move in any direction. The ideal, of course, would be Canadian ownership. I think we are all concerned about the effect of non-ownership of our resources in Canada, particularly our energy resources and our natural resources. There are varying views. I was very impressed by the effective speech by the hon. member, I believe for Don Valley, who feels that we should not worry too much about ownership of resources, that resources are resources are resources, and should concentrate Canadian savings in things like book publishing and such which do make Canada unique. That is one view.
There is a limited amount of Canadian savings. We should not kid ourselves above this. I believe even the most nationalistic of economy nationalists say we need continued foreign investment in greater proportion than before. The question is, how do we get that foreign investment in such a way that it does not involve ownership of our country and does not affect our ability to direct our own destiny. In respect of a pipeline, if we do not own it, is this one of the things which would inhibit our ability to develop this country as we see fit. This is a question to which I believe ail hon. members must address themselves. We might ask ourselves whether it would be good to have a great proportion of Canadian savings in the next few years end up in the pipeline and not be available for such things in the public sector as guaranteed incomes, public well-being and so on, or for the book publishing business and other things in the private sector, bearing in mind that this pipeline may be over Canadian territory.

WEST INDIES-REQUEST FOR IMPROVEMENT IN TRADE AND CULTURAL RELATIONS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of taking an initiative in seeking to promote closer and more harmonious relations with the Commonwealth Caribbean through the convening of heads-of-government or ministerial conference, efforts to increase trade between the region and Canada, strengthening cultural ties and generally an upgrading of priority for this region in Canadian foreign policy consideration.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is not for me a new subject, or a new interest. As many of my colleagues know, I have several times before raised this general question,, although previously in a different terminology. I think I have reached something of an apogee of excellence in my phraseology this time! My great concern in this general question is simply that we must raise the priority which we give to the Commonwealth Caribbean in our foreign policy. This is the underlying aspect in all my presentations on this very important and interesting subject. The area to which I wish to draw the attention of Your Honour and that of my colleagues is a small area but it is one with large problems. It is an area which has all the difficulties or nearly all the difficulties facing emerging nations across the world. All the economic pains of the developing states are found in the Commonwealth Caribbean. They, too, have these intensive and intense questions of race, color and identity which are such vital questions and often such difficult probing questions in today's sensitive world.
But these communities have something else which should mean a great deal to parliamentarians of our tradition. The political institutions of the Commonwealth Caribbean, in the face of many assaults, have stood well, and are, I believe, a magnificent tribute to the type of political institutions which are of the same general structure as our own. In looking at this area, I think we should never forget that in the area of political institutions we have much in common. We are of the same mould, and our Commonwealth parliamentary relationships with these people are, as they should be, of the closest.
Since I last spoke, there have been developments in the Commonwealth Caribbean; there have been incidents and occurrences which some Canadians have viewed with great anxiety as indications of considerable distress.
March 29, 1971

There have been riots and protests against Canadian property in Trinidad and Tobago. I must point out that it was not only Canadian property at which the excitement of the people who were at that time moving about the streets was directed. There have been demonstrations with some anti-Canadian undertones or overtones, and there have been some sharp criticisms of Canadian policies on other occasions. Not that I believe or think that Canadians should believe that they are somehow immune from criticism or that throughout the world we should be universally loved and everlastingly adored. We think it is quite normal that there should be such a thing as anti-Americanism, but surely we cannot be immune from criticism and misunderstanding, so I am not disturbed by these incidents. It would however, be a mistake to overemphasize the incidents and to regard them as typifying any deep hatred or continuing hostility toward Canada. To take such a view, to make such a judgment would be, I believe, most unwise. But to pass them off as a mere nothing, to pretend that nothing really had happened, is, in my opinion, equally erroneous. We must not and cannot take these neighbours for granted-neighbours never should. They have grievances, and I am glad that they are expressing themselves with candor and sometimes with feeling.
As I said in the House at the time that the unilateral decision regarding the termination of the 29 cent sugar subsidy was announced, it was a bad thing because it was announced, and it was terrible because it was done unilaterally. It was a boober of major proportions, and I am glad that the government, which deserved censure for doing it, backtracked, changed its mind and left the subsidy at least for a year, and I hope it will be longer than a year, until adequate, thoughtful and sensible arrangements can be made.
There are problems regarding immigration, although I am convinced that our policies in immigration today are far better than they used to be, but there are still some difficulties and misunderstandings. Many people in the Commonwealth Caribbean sometimes suggest that we are willing to accept only those people whose contribution to their own lands would be most valuable. Knowing the dreary and painful story of the migration of the people from the Maritime provinces to other areas in North America, I have much sympathy for these feelings.
When in Barbados a few weeks ago-and as I look outside today I wish I had been able to stay-many people asked me why Canada had no mission in Bridgetown, in view of the fact that Barbados has a very fine high commission office in Ottawa. This is one situation which I greet with incredulity and with embarrassment. Surely, our austerity is not so compelling that we cannot afford to open a mission in the friendly and beautiful country of Barbados where so many Canadians are involved personally, financially and as residents. Indeed, it is an area of most extensive Canadian interest and involvement. Of course we should reciprocate and open a Barbados mission right away. We have fine missions in Trinidad, Tobago and Jamaica. I had the opportunity of visiting these people not long ago, but I think it is unfortunate that it was found necessary to cut down the
Trade Relations with West Indies
personnel of these important missions. I recognize that good work has been done, and our country is generally well regarded in the area, not just for that oblique and negative virtue of our not being Englishmen or Americans, a kind of compliment which I never find very satisfying. I hope this is not the case.
The need is great and the opportunities for more service are immense in the area. In an earlier Parliament when presenting this subject I quoted a learned Canadian scholar, Professor Kontak from St. Francis Xavier University, who knows the West Indies and the Commonwealth Caribbean well. Professor Kontak returned from a recent extended visit to the Commonwealth Caribbean and reported that the friendship he found for Canada was almost unbelievable. He said:
This friendship gives a feeling of both pride and embarrassment; pride because Canada has conducted her affairs in such a way as to produce this feeling, and embarrassment because she has done so little compared to what she is capable of and can afford to do.
I cannot summarize in a better way my own feeling with reference to our stake in the area and our opportunities in the region. Although I come from a part of Canada that has long been neglected-and may I say in candor never more than by the present government-I do not join those who believe that cutting off foreign aid would somehow, some way, miraculously bring us internal prosperity. Such is not the case. We must, even in a selfish way, take an interest and become involved in other parts of what is sometimes called this global village. But having said that, I reiterate a statement that I have often made since I came to the House of Commons, and that is one of doubt that Canada with its resources can mount meaningful programs of aid to 65 to 70 countries across the world. It cannot be done.
In many cases it is a mere drop in the bucket. So, we must select areas where we can hope to be effective. I believe that no part of the world with which we have contact, for which we are concerned, and in which we have an interest deserves a higher priority than the Commonwealth Caribbean. In this important area we can, I believe, not only be effective, but in some parts of the Commonwealth Caribbean our aid, our interest, our assistance and our friendship could indeed be decisive as some of the communities, whose political and economic viability is very precarious, struggle with problems and cope with difficulties which might very easily overwhelm their institutions, assault their stability, and create the kind of conditions which would bring no good to them, no good to Canada, and no good to those people who believe in a peaceful free world.
My motion endeavours to set out some areas in which I think we can do more. I have been very worried for some time that the high water mark of 1966, when the former Prime Minister, Mr. Pearson, assembled in Ottawa a heads of government conference, was much higher than the level we are now performing upon. I believe we should have taken the initiative in assuring that there would be another heads of government meeting in our

March 29, 1971
Trade Relations with West Indies
time, or at least ministerial meetings, to indicate, to underscore and to re-emphasize the concern we have lor this area.
I believe we can strengthen our ties through parliamentary delegations. When I was in Port-of-Spain I was impressed to hear the Speaker of the Lower House and the President of the Upper House suggest that we should develop a pattern of exchanges between our legislative bodies and theirs. I hope it will be possible for this kind of initiative to be followed. I believe there are great opportunities for more cultural exchanges. I remember so vividly the magnificent performance of the wonderful calypso group who came up to Canada in 1967. Now, I am expecting to see another group which I believe the governments of Trinidad, and Tobago have indicated they will send, as they have been the winners of the great carnival contest.
Students have done a splendid job. Students from the West Indies, from the Commonwealth Caribbean area, have long been in our universities. I have seen them in my classes years ago. I have the highest regard for them. I think we should be doing more now in trying through our programs to assist students who would remain, for at least a large part of their course, down in institutions in that area.
We can also increase trade. I do not pretend that the opportunities are immense, or that it is a tremendous area of growth. And we do have to take into consideration changing tastes and changing technology. But there is ground for a substantial improvement. I believe, particularly, we should assist in increasing and stimulating the flow of seaborne commerce. Perhaps we are entering a new era where we must look to the riches in the sea, on the sea, and under the sea, and become more conscious of those possibilities. This is why I suppose we from the Atlantic provinces have long known the charm of the West Indies and the value of friendship with them.
Also important in the whole Canadian program with respect to the Commonwealth Caribbean is the work done by the individuals down there, sent by CDA and CUSO, and by the other group, the retired executives, CESO which some nasty person has called the paunch corps. There are many stimulating and interesting experiments being carried out there. In Jamaica, in their capital city, the Casa Monte hotel has been turned into a school for hotel training, run by a former dean of Ryerson Institute. A fine job is being done by that man, and by many Canadians who have outstanding experience in the hotel field here.
Canadian agriculturalists are helping with a program of agricultural development, especially in the raising of cattle. I discovered down there some fine Canadian Holstein cattle, which are being bred in the islands. I only ask one question: why weren't there more from Prince Edward Island, which is very famous for its Holstein cattle?
But to move from agriculture to teaching, I think there we get to the real ambassadors. I can well remember the vice-principal of the Manchester teacher training school, in Manchester, Jamaica, telling us one and all at a meeting that without its Canadian friends the school would have had to close long ago. Every year one meets and hears of bright Canadian people, interested Canadian people, outward looking Canadian young people who are down there doing a fine job.
I suggest again, as I did on motions the other day, that we do make a mistake in one respect. When we send people to various parts of the world they are given a briefing by the Department of External Affairs but when they come back, full of knowledge, and enriched with concern, no one pays any attention to them. The department should find ways to communicate with these people and draw on their knowledge, experience and concern.
We should and must do more. It may be unusual for a member of this House to enter into salutations to the other house, but I am convinced the finest study done on this question for a long, long time was that by the foreign affairs committee of the Senate. I commend their exercise. I support their recommendations. I believe they are giving leadership in a path which we should follow, namely, to do more, to think more on this whole question, and we will all benefit as we strengthen our bonds with the Commonwealth Caribbean.
