speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I fully support the motion put forward by the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie). It is rather difficult to follow him in the debate because he has covered the subject so well. Those of us who were here in 1966 when there was a conference between the Canadian government and the Caribbean governments had great hopes at that time. We expected a dramatic improvement in relations between Canada and the Commonwealth Caribbean countries. I must be frank and state that the results to date have not come up to our expectations. It is true that there have been improvements in some areas, but there has been deterioration in others.
As a member from Montreal, I cannot help but be aware of the riots which we had at Sir George Williams University. We have a large number of Caribbean immigrants in Montreal. I have been in touch with them often I have many friends among the Caribbean community, but I repeat that while there have been certain advances, in some areas there has been deterioration.
I endorse the suggestion made by the hon. member for Hillsborough that another conference between Canada and Commonwealth Caribbean countries be held at the heads of government level. Last fall the Hon. Paul Martin, the Leader of the Senate and a member of the cabinet, visited some 13 countries and territories in the Caribbean area. He made an effort to follow up on many of the matters that had been discussed previously, and to bring about improved relations with those governments. The report on his trip can be found in the statement which he made in the Senate on December 8, 1970, and which was recorded in the Senate Hansard of that date at page 293. It was a very extensive report.
In addition, in 1970 we had the report of the Senate Committee on Canadian Caribbean relations. While I also congratulate the Senate and support most of its recommendations, I think we must realize that the evidence

March 29, 1971

which formed the basis of that report was evidence that was taken mainly from a Canadian perspective. If I remember my reading of the report correctly, I think all the witnesses were Canadians or non-Caribbean citizens. The report is valuable but I think more is needed.
In 1970 we also had the publication of the government's policy statements on foreign policy, but no special mention was made of the Commonwealth Caribbean. I agree with the report of the Senate and with the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) when he said that the Commonwealth Caribbean should be given a special place in our foreign policy. I want to emphasize that, Mr. Speaker. The grounds for that special place were put forward when we had a conference in 1966 but were not followed up in the way we expected. The basis for that special place is primarily due to the fact that the Commonwealth Caribbean countries-as a matter of fact all Caribbean countries-are our neighbours and we share many things. We have historical ties in trade; we were both colonies of Great Britain; we share social and political institutions and, above all, we need each other. There are things that they can help us with and vice versa. These increased relations, Mr. Speaker, have to be carried on as neighbour to neighbour and friend to friend, as equals and not in a neo-colonial way nor a paternalistic way.
The areas where increased relations can take place, and these have been referred to in the motion, are areas of trade, aid, foreign investment and tourism. With respect to aid, the goal must be to develop the independence of these people. It should primarily be aid without strings, untied aid. It should be directed to the self-fulfilment of people living in these areas. Following on that, if we are serious in our aid programs, there must be trade. We cannot pretend to assist people, put money into their country so that they can develop, and then refuse to trade with them; trade is extremely important. The mistake we made with the sugar agreement was corrected, but I think it is important that in all trade relations with the Caribbean countries we work as partners and with full consultation.
Some of the most sensitive areas have been in the field of foreign investment. Canada and Canadian private companies are very visible in the Commonwealth Caribbean. You don't have to go very far to see that our banks, the aluminium company, many of the hotels and a lot of the tourist industry are Canadian owned and operated. In the past there has been criticism that Canadian companies operating in the Caribbean have not provided enough participation at the local level; that wages were at the minimum level; that not enough attention was paid to enlightened employer-employee relations nor to the wishes of the people as expressed in their local legislatures and local government. I think this is being corrected. I think Canadian companies operating in the Caribbean are aware of the aspirations of the people and are trying to correct some of the failings of the past.
The Senate Committee made several good recommendations which I think are worth while. In the area of
Trade Relations with West Indies Canadian government machinery, they suggested that the Interdepartmental Committee on Canada-Commonwealth Caribbean Relations should be given a clear and precise mandate to maintain a continuing overview of current and long term issues. They felt it was necessary that there be a co-ordinating agency within the Canadian government which would treat the Caribbean area as a special area. Another important recommendation was that there should be established in Canada a Caribbean marketing agency. This recommendation reads:
The Canadian government should suggest the establishment of a joint Canada-Caribbean marketing agency to be funded initially as required by Canada. Such an agency could conduct market surveys, establish distribution contracts, advertise and generally promote complementary two-way trade. This could be a relatively low cost assistance project yielding substantial and lasting results for the Caribbean countries. By selecting promising export products, (examples at this time would include bananas, rum, and certain citrus products), the agency could have a highly beneficial impact.
Then, there is tourism, Mr. Speaker, and this is an area which is likely to be sensitive. Very often Canadians take the point of view that all the tourism that is directed to the Caribbean countries by Canadians is valuable. It can be touchy when Canadians live in very luxurious hotels in those countries, often to the benefit of the Canadian hotel owners and the Canadian tourists, without too much benefit going to the countries themselves. I thought the Senate Committee made some worth-while points on this issue as well when they said, at page xxii of their report:
Evidence given before the committee indicated that tourism has had a number of undesirable social side-effects without necessarily bringing all the expected economic benefits. The committee recognizes that the responsibility for solving these problems rests primarily with the local governments, but has several specific proposals to make.
The committee goes on to suggest that goods and services required by the tourist industry should be purchased in the Caribbean countries, so that the industry will stimulate secondary and tertiary effects in the economy. This is a worth-while recommendation.
In the area of immigration we see a considerable increase from the Caribbean over the last few years, especially in Montreal. Many outstanding citizens have come to us from the Caribbean but there is that touchy problem of "brain drain". Sometimes we are in a dilemma to know whether we should encourage the best trained people to come to Canada when they might be needed in their own countries. On the one hand, we are helping the university of the West Indies to train people but often we find the best ones coming to Canada. Mr. Speaker, I will make just a brief intervention. I join the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) in extending congratulations to the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) for presenting this resolution to the House.
I wish to comment on two matters with regard to our special relationship with the Caribbean arising out of a common language and underlying cultural affinity. This is an ideal field for Canada to work closely with area governments concerned to develop policies of a pilot nature which could then be employed in furthering our relationships with other nations of the world. If this argument sounds involved, I will attempt to be more specific.
Any developed nation which attempts to establish relationships with developing nations, and in so doing provides economic assistance through public means and private capital, encounters the difficulty-such as we have seen in the Caribbean-of eventually becoming charged with embarking upon neo-imperialist policies. Because of the special affinities between the Caribbean and Canada, the Caribbean is an ideal area for us to begin working out ways of avoiding this particular problem, which will become greater because over the past years our government has become committed to a policy of increasing the amount of foreign aid to other countries.
Could we not use our special relationship with the Caribbean, in consultation with the area governments, to attempt to develop ways and means of providing the assistance they require which will not carry with it charges of neo-imperialism? Could we not develop ways and means of ensuring that Canadian private investment in the Caribbean area meets with the criteria for economic self-development and the maintenance and control of their own economies which the Caribbean would like to see? In short, could we not put some special effort into the particular problems of this area in the hope that the formulas thus established would have wider application?
The second matter which I wish to draw to the attention of the House is one in which we might have some success in developing a pilot project in conjunction with the Commonwealth Caribbean nations. I refer to immigration. The two previous speakers have indicated the problem with regard to immigration. We tend to skim off the cream of developing countries by bringing their best educated people to our country. In this way we are dealing an economic blow to the country which has spent money to educate these people to the extent that they become acceptable under our immigration laws. At the same time, we are doing very little to assist those countries in dealing with the many problems they have with regard to the vast numbers of lesser skilled people.
In consultation with the Caribbean governments we could develop a pilot project whereby Canada would undertake to bring in certain numbers of people who do not meet our strict immigration requirements. This could be done on the clear understanding that the government of Canada would undertake to provide them with the necessary training and education to live within our boundaries. I am not speaking of a program of bringing in vast numbers of people; I am simply suggesting a pilot program which could be worked out in the Caribbean area where there is so much in the nature of cultural and linguistic affinities, the results of which could eventually be applied in other areas of the world.
While I have not stated these suggestions in a detailed form, they are in keeping with the suggestions in the resolution of the hon. member for Hillsborough. I hope that some member of the government will find time to examine these suggestions to see if acceptable programs of the type I have suggested could be worked out in detail.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my intervention will be very brief. I think there are at least three other members who want to speak. There have been three very thoughtful speeches on this important resolution. I concur with a great many of the points raised by the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie). The hon. member raised three specific points in his speech which was filled with important points, which is typical of the hon. member.
One suggestion, which was reinforced by the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) was basically sound. We should not be diverted from maintaining close relations with the Commonwealth Caribbean countries because of unpleasant instances, such as occurred in Montreal, or difficulties which Canadians or Canadian institutions encounter in the Commonwealth Caribbean countries. These are often short-term difficulties which are associated with problems of development and relations between developing and developed countries. This is an important point.
The hon. member for Hillsborough stated that we should not yield to the misguided pressure that comes from some quarters-that charity begins at home. He stated that aid should not be viewed as a charitable operation. Relations between developing and developed countries are mutually advantageous, even self-serving.

March 29, 1971

Where aid is involved, this is part of a process which helps the developed countries as well as the developing countries, particularly through developing new markets. When the claim is made that we have problems in our own country which should be attended to, we should not be diverted from the main thrust and purpose of foreign aid programs, albeit that some of our problems are compelling and must receive attention. However, one cannot be solved at the expense of the other. It is up to the members of this House to maintain the balance in public argument on this question.
Another interesting point which the hon. member raised was that our institutions are similar and our problems as legislators are in some ways common. He stated that we should have more contact with each other, not simply during the winter months. I would certainly welcome a month's sojourn in the Barbados. He stated that at times convenient to both sides we should meet and discuss mutual problems. He stated that when parliamentary delegations visit these countries, there should be some form of follow-up approach with the Department of External Affairs. The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Skoberg) is in the chamber. On at least one occasion we have travelled together on an important mission. We were very gratified by the fact that following a mission a real interest was shown by the Department of External Affairs. There could be an important input from parliamentary delegations who have visited abroad.
I disagree with the hon. member for Hillsborough and the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace that our relations with the Commonwealth Caribbean countries are not developing. I found his argument difficult to accept. Furthermore, it is not clear to me what both hon. members mean when they talk about a special case in our foreign policy. Listening to their speeches, I did not detect supporting arguments for this contention. The only way in which the degree of priority attached to the Commonwealth Caribbean can be judged is by the facts-and it seems to me the facts are impressive. I will return to this point.
In his resolution, the hon. member for Hillsborough made an issue of one point. To quote from the motion before us, he argues that close and more harmonious relations should be brought about with the Caribbean through convening conferences between heads of state or ministers. Personally, I do not feel strongly either for or against meetings of ministers or heads of state. I have an idea that this type of arrangement is no more effective than the kind of close bilateral contacts we presently have with the Caribbean. I do not think it can be argued that because we have not convened successive conferences between heads of state or ministers our ties with the Caribbean are not rated as of first-rank importance by the Canadian government. I happen to support bilateral relations of the kind being pursued at the present time; I believe they are more effective.
I should like to put on record an indication of the extent and complexity of our present ties, because this is the only way in which we are able to judge the impor-
Trade Relations with West Indies tance the government attaches to the relations between Canada and the Caribbean at the present time. I think we ought to review the extent and complexity of Canadian interests in the area, both governmental and private. At present it is estimated that there is $450 million to $550 million in Canadian investment in the region. During 1970 Canadian exports reached $134.1 million as compared with $113 million in 1969, and imports totalled $77.9 million as compared with $108.7 million in 1969. In the past five years over $100 million has been allocated to the Commonwealth Caribbean under the Canadian development assistance program, including $24 million in 1970-71.
At present there are over 3,000 Canadians living as permanent residents in the region, and over 125,000 Canadians visit the islands annually. During 1970 nearly 14,000 West Indians emigrated to Canada. Here is the best kind of cultural exchange-an exchange of people. There are Canadian High Commissions in Jamaica, Trinidad, Tobago and Guyana, and these three countries, plus Barbados, maintain High Commissions in O.tawa. The Leeward and Windward Islands have a commissioner in Montreal.
Consider our development assistance program. I am reciting this because I believe it is a basic fact upon which hon. members can judge whether or not priority is given to our relationship with the Commonwealth West Indies. In the 1970-71 fiscal year, $24 million were allocated to the Commonwealth Caribbean, with a major concentration in the sectors of education, transportation, water and sewage systems, and civil aviation, including airports and infrastructure. In addition to specific projects in individual countries, assistance within the aid allocation I have outlined is being provided to the multinational University of the West Indies and to the University of Guyana.
On a per capita basis, the Commonwealth Caribbean is the largest recipient of any region receiving Canadian development assistance. This is the point I am making. If we are to assess whether relations are developing or deteriorating, one can best do so in terms of facts such as I have put on record. This brings me to a point which was raised by the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace.
The relationship between a developing country and a developed country poses extremely difficult problems for both. If we go beyond the pious sentiments we express from time to time about the need for assisting developing countries, we are bound to think intelligently about what we mean by trade. We cannot simply provide assistance to help build up a domestic industry, and then exclude from our markets the exports of the country concerned. I suggest that hon. members look closely at the results of the UNCTAD conference, or take a look at the Algerian resolution setting out the demands of the developing countries in terms of their trade relationship with the developed countries.
As I say, the difficulties attached to these relationships are great. All of us have industries in our constituencies which would be affected by any meaningful easing of import restrictions. All of us have constituents employed in Canadian industry who would be affected if we were

Decisions in this area are hard to make-but I hope we have gone beyond the stage of rhetoric, the stage at which we are prepared only to talk piously about assistance, and have reached the point at which we ask ourselves what precisely we are prepared to do to allow developing countries to sell their products to us. Mr. Speaker, I wish to join my hon. friend from Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) and others in saying a few words about this proposal. I congratulate my hon. friend, not only because his motion is in front of us today but because this distinguished member of the House has spent a great part of his life voicing concern about the relationship between Canada and those delightful islands not too far south of us.
With respect to the delightfulness of the islands, I have yet to be made aware of any government aid having anything to do with my desire to be in the Caribbean during the wintertime. It is just that on occasion it is a hell of a lot more delightful down there than it is here. I had intended to make other comments to reinforce the arguments of my colleague who brought this matter to our attention, particularly with respect to the absence of representation in Bridgetown, but I think trade is a useful way to measure the reality of our relationships and the concern we have for them.
A previous speaker asked us not to get carried away by our own rhetoric, but I cannot resist answering him by saying that although he left us with the impression that there has been an increase in trade-true, there has-the relative impact of trade in general and the relative position of our fish and flour exports to the Caribbean in terms of their imports are the true measure of our concern. Our trade with the Caribbean has been going down. Our flour exports to the Caribbean are away down, even though consumption of flour on the islands has not gone down. I am not saying whose fault it is. In many instances it may be the fault of our own entrepreneurs. Perhaps we should have encouraged Canadians to build flour mills in the Caribbean; but we backed away from this, and I should like to know why.
I do not want to isolate flour from other commodities. Let me take fish. Traditionally, Canada has supplied much of the fish eaten in the Caribbean area, but in recent years, while in absolute terms trade has gone up, in relative terms our share of the market has gone down. Perhaps this is because we have not catered to the increasing sophistication of taste and well-being on the part of the residents of the islands. Perhaps we have taken them for granted. Perhaps we are continuing to take them too much for granted and this is why our relative trade picture has worsened. Perhaps we have not done enough to encourage imports of certain fruits and other traditional north-south trade commodities for hundreds of years. It is to this point that I wish to address myself.
Throughout my life in Halifax-and, I suspect, the lives of my great, great grandparents too-our Maritimes relations with this part of the world have been warm and continuous. But it is here, at the level of the central government, that the emphasis must be placed? The degree of our interest in the Caribbean must find its source of authority here, not in the Maritimes. I said a moment ago that our declining trade picture is not our fault. I could have mentioned meats. Why cannot we compete with Australia and New Zealand in meat exports to Caribbean countries? Why have we not done those things that encourage, at the senior minister level, an ever closer and growing relationship between Canada and the Commonwealth Caribbean? Why have we been satisfied to rest on the success of bilateral relationships? I suggest this is no way to measure the degree of concern that we should have for our friends in the Caribbean. I have spent a number of years in that part of the world, very delightful years. I have also spent some time in South America. But never have I sensed, in and around the islands, anything but good will toward Canada. Nevertheless, from my own personal experience in the area, not to mention the evidence we have had in recent years, the fact is we are not paying the attention to the Caribbean that we should and could without any cost to ourselves.
As the hon. member for Hillsborough said, there should be more consultation and meetings at a higher level, to the mutual benefit of us both. We would not be the benefactors, as was the impression left by the speaker who has just resumed his seat. We are two separate entities who enjoy very much in common. But we are in a position to do much more. We are in a position to take advantage of our ability to do more, to do that which we have failed to do. In the narrow area of trade, the fact that while our trade has increased, its relative position in the Commonwealth Caribbean has diminished must be the measure of our sincerity.

Mr. Chairman, I thank hon. members for being so patient with my rather lengthy review of the matters raised in questions posed by hon. members. I have tried to the best of my ability to answer at least the major questions asked by hon. gentlemen opposite. May I finish the point I was making at five o'clock respecting foreign ownership. Although we have stressed that Canadian ownership would be one of the ingredients which would receive preference under the guidelines, we have purposely not made any complete, final and definitive resolution as to the quantum or nature of the ownership because we did not known the complete economics of such pipeline or pipelines. We wanted that decision to be made when applicants came forward with active propositions.
Very likely, this will be a single applicant because of the magnitude of the enterprise. We can determine at that time whether the degree of Canadian ownership is sufficient. If it is clear from the economics of the project that we might either have to take a certain degree of Canadian ownership or postpone the project, or not go ahead with it for the time being, if it were not feasible in any other way, the decision would have to be made at that time. To make the decision in advance, before knowing what the economic connotations of the pipeline are, we thought would be prejudging the issue before we had the facts with which to judge it.
As I was saying at five o'clock, we must determine our priorities for Canadian ownership or, if you like, the gradual improvement of Canadian ownership in our resources and in our Canadian industrial complex generally. We can then determine whether we want this quantum, be it at $5 billion, $4 billion or $8 billion, to be made up of Canadian savings in pipelines, or whether we prefer to have that amount of money put into other areas of Canadian ownership. I was pointing out that the line will be on Canadian territory, subject to Canadian law, subject to Canadian regulatory agencies and, no doubt, the subject matter of some pre-existing agreements either with the companies or with the United States
Government Organization Act, 1970 government which will determine in large measure the responsibilities of the line for the carrying of Canadian products. It may be that this will be one area in which we will not require the quantum or percentage of Canadian ownership that we feel is essential in other Canadian resources or industrial entities.
Again I say that we have in some measure left that question open, but with a clear indication that the matter of Canadian content in all forms, including that of financial ownership, will be very much in our minds. An application with the provision of maximum Canadian ownership would quite clearly receive priority over an application with provision for a lesser content of Canadian ownership.
May I briefly deal with one other point which was raised by hon. members, the question of gas reserves. This is a very important question, and I would not want to leave in the air any question or suggestion that the government had any doubts as to the capabilities of the National Energy Board in determining gas reserves before making its decision to permit gas exports. I think the record of the National Energy Board is an extremely good one; it has been extremely good in the period that the board has served the Canadian public. I think the board has been right in a large percentage of times although, as in any other human institutions, it may be wrong from time to time. But it has been more often right than wrong. With regard to the question of gas reserves which the board determines to be available for Canadian use, present and future, before declaring a surplus for export, I think it is extremely important for the record to be kept clear. The estimates of the National Energy Board, of the requirements of Canada as indicated in their decision of August, 1970, in the matter of export applications, make substantial allowances for an increasing share in the Canadian market for natural gas.
Specifically, the estimates provided for, (a) the expansion of services to Vancouver Island, (b) a generous allowance for thermal electric use in British Columbia, which is not used at the present time, (c) a total allowance for Alberta, almost identical to the estimates made by the Alberta Oil and gas conservation board, (d) an allowance for Saskatchewan to support a much higher level of potash production than foreseen by some of the applicants for export licences, and (e) an allowance for the use of natural gas in the Hearne plant of Ontario and two possible other hydro plants.
The National Energy Board, in declaring the quantum of gas which could be declared surplus to Canadian requirements, and thus available for export, sought to establish an amount equal to approximately 30 years of Canadian need at the current level of demand. It may be argued that this amount is not enough or is too much, but I would point out that in the producing areas some people feel that this is far too conservative an estimate. They have argued that this would inhibit exploration and thus, in the long run, diminish the reserves that would be available for Canada.
So we can have the argument both ways. It may be argued that this amount is not enough, or is too much.

March 29, 1971
Government Organization Act, 1970 However, in the board's judgment it was the correct amount to set aside for future Canadian requirements and the government relied on the board's judgment. I am prepared to back the board against any so-called experts upon whom others feel they can rely. In this regard, I might say the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands indicated he relied on other experts. His view of the board's judgment was the opposite to that of those in Alberta who contend the board was too cautious and, hence, inhibited growth. The hon. member's experts apparently are of the opinion that the board was too optimistic and should have kept much more gas for Canadian use in inventory.
If there is such a group of experts, I am sure the government and the board would be glad to hear from them and compare their expert judgment to that of the very great expertise which exists on the board. But until we hear from experts whose credentials are more notable and whose record is established as being superior to that of the board, or whose argument is so profound as to indicate the board was wrong in its judgment, I think we can and should rely on the judgment of the National Energy Board in this regard.
My hon. friend frowns on exporting that which is surplus to Canadian needs. Perhaps I might examine the economics in respect of no further exports of surplus. As I indicated, in respect of the non-export of oil there will be a substantial cost of holding the surplus in inventory. The Canadian Petroleum Association has estimated that it would cost $3 million to carry one trillion cubic feet in inventory for one year. That, of course, is a cost that would be borne by the consumers of gas be they Canadian or others, and most of the gas-I believe some 60 per cent or more-is consumed by Canadian consumers. These consumers would, of course, bear the cost of holding the gas. The price of holding these resources in Canada in the long run, as I say, would have to be borne by Canadian consumers through much higher prices and a decrease in additions to reserves because of reduced cash flow to producers and explorers.
My hon. friend also asked what proportion of the readily accessible gas is being held in reserve for the use of Canadians. I would point out that some 36 trillion cubic feet, or two-thirds of the established reserves of 54 trillion cubic feet, are dedicated to the Canadian market. The Canadian Petroleum Association estimates the potential reserves of gas in Canada are 725 trillion cubic feet. Reserves found to date represent only about 9 per cent of Canada's potential reserves and, as I say, two-thirds of those are held for the Canadian domestic market.
I might also briefly refer to the hon. gentleman's concern in respect of the recent hearings of the board at which the president of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines indicated there was insufficient gas to satisfy the needs of current application. I would point out that as a result of hearings and subsequent investigation, the board has found-and the decision of the board is now public record-that Trans-Canada has sufficient gas to meet the requirements of application and could deliver the gas to satisfy those particular contracts.

First, I would point out that this is the report of the staff of the National Energy Board and is not binding on the board itself sitting as a judicial or quasi-judicial body. The board, of course, is not bound by the findings. Its staff is presenting this report, so that the Canadian public generally, the parliament of Canada and potential consumers might be advised of the prognostications in respect of supply and demand. The board in each case, however, must be satisfied by any evidence current at the particular hearing as to what reserves are available on that particular day.
I think this should resolve any qualms hon. members might have that this report of the board's staff is in any way binding on the board in any future hearings. It is merely an information document which is available to the people of Canada and to parliament concerning the prognostication for energy supply and demand.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands had some concern that in the 1990 prognostication the board indicated that the demand for natural gas in Canada would be, on a per capita basis, the same as that which existed in the United States in 1975. He found, by reason of our climate, that there was something inordinate in this conclusion. Might I point out that, again, these are the prognostications of the staff and are not binding upon the board. That conclusion was based upon the premise that some 42 per cent of Canada's energy needs in 1990 would be met by electricity generated in Canada, whereas in the same period in 1990 the prognostications are that only some 9 per cent or 10 per cent, if memory serves me correctly, of the United States demands for energy will be met by electricity. This possibly is the reason, in making its conclusions, that the board's staff determined that a far higher percentage of the needs would have to be met by natural gas in the United States.

Mr. Chairman, as the hon. member quite properly says, the land use regulations under the Territorial Lands Act do not come within the purview of my responsibilities. Quite apart from any possibility of a pipeline, I think that if an undertaking were given it would be fulfilled as soon as possible by the government or the responsible minister. I want to assure the hon. member, whose concern in these matters is not of recent vintage and who has shown a great interest particularly in the ecological problems affecting these questions, that prior to any hearing taking place before the National Energy Board the government's ground rules and the basis for them will be made very clear.
I might point out that this has been a very different situation from 1956 when, as I understand it, the debate in respect of the construction of the pipeline was probably the first opportunity Parliament had to get its teeth into the problem. I would point out that since then we have had the National Energy Board Act. Many hon. members have evidenced their concern that there should be a hearing. I do not know whether there will be other hearings. There may be other hearings; for instance, to determine problems peculiar to the administration of the Northwest Territories. But certainly there will be hearings before the National Energy Board, something which was not the order of the day in 1956.
The application of any applicant before the National Energy Board will be a matter of public record, a public document, a public application which can be studied by any interested members or by the public. Any government decision affecting the hearing will be made public well ahead of any hearing, and certainly any member of the public or any public organization will have full right to appear at such hearing. There may never be a hearing about an oil pipeline in our lifetime, as I think we have made clear in our discussions with the industry. We have no assurance whatsoever that any application will be made with respect to an oil pipeline; so it may be that all our debate here will have turned out to be in vain, although it has been a very useful debate.
If such an application does ever come, I think it is extremely important that the House has considered all aspects of the possibilities well ahead of the event. And I believe, in my humble judgment, that there will be an application about a gas line. I think the economics of a gas line are very much a probability. I can only assure the hon. member that before such a hearing takes place we will make public any government determinations, including the land use regulations, if they are applicable, or such rulings apart from the regulations as may be made by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development with regard to the location of the pipeline. We will consider the corridor, etc., so that all members will have the maximum knowledge and information available to them prior to the hearing. Therefore, this public hearing, which will be available to the people of Canada prior to such an important decision, will in fact be a useful public hearing wherein there is maximum information and, hence, maximum capability not only to hon. members but to Canadians generally to make their views known to that tribunal.

speechtext:
The proposal before us under this clause states that there shall be a Post Office and there shall be a Postmaster General. The point is that the Postmaster General shall be a full member of the cabinet. As far as Postmaster Generals go, Mr. Chairman, they go very rapidly. In the past 14 years we have had nine or 10 Postmasters General; I have lost count. The turnover of Postmasters General takes place at an almost indecent rate. This is one of the few things that is weakening the generally good record of our Post Office.
It might be worth while spending a few moments to discuss this great public enterprise which we operate, the Post Office of Canada. The Post Office Department handles close to five billion pieces of mail every year. It serves five million doors across the country. It employs 47,000 people and operates some 9,000 branch post offices. Financially, the last figures I have indicate that the Post Office takes in approximately $444 million a year. Out of that it is losing almost $52 million a year, $1 million a week. This sounds like a great deal of money to lose. In a way it is. But if we consider that we have between 20 million and 22 million Canadians which the Post Office serves, the loss per capita is not very great.
If we divide $1 million per week by 21 million or 22 million Canadians, the Post office is operating at a loss of
Government Organization Act, 1970
between four cents and five cents per capita each week. More than half of that four or five cents per week per capita is generated by the loss on second-class mail; that is, mail put out for commercial reasons in the hope of profit.
Over the years the Post Office has consistently done well with regard to carrying the ordinary first-class letters which it was basically set up to deliver. It has operated in this category either at a small profit or at a small loss. At the present time I estimate that the loss on first-class mail amounts to less than one cent per capita. But the Post Office has consistently lost on second-class mail, and this has long been a subject of criticism by the Auditor General and the Public Accounts Committee which have recommended that steps be taken to deal with this situation. Lest anyone assume I am suggesting that the postal loss with regard to second-class mail results from carrying small weekly newspapers, I wish to add that this loss amounts to but $2.3 million a year out of a total of $27 million in connection with profit-motivated mail.
These are some of the broad outlines of the postal business we are operating. It is a vast business, and we should consider that its purpose and use to our country goes beyond exact calculation in terms of dollars and cents. It would not be wrong to say that our postal system is contributing something to our national identity in the same way as the CBC is doing in another field. Dollars and cents are important matters to take into consideration, but one ought not to measure what the Post Office is doing strictly on that basis.
In some respects there is something very odd about the way in which the Post Office operates. For example, the public pays, through the Department of Public Works, for the accommodation of post offices across Canada. This charge is borne by the public in addition to what it pays in the course of buying postage stamps. The postal buildings are free to the Post Office. On the other hand, the Post Office performs services for a variety of departments and also to members of Parliament, for example, who enjoy free mailing facilities during the session. My view is that this is a quaint and curious situation which should be changed. In this respect we should be able to place the postal service on a strictly business basis, on a dollar and cents level.
I have drawn attention to the fact that the great loss to the Post Office is incurred in the area of second-class mail. This loss amounts to about 2 to 2J cents per capita per week. If it desired to reduce this cost we should consider whether the second-class mail rate should be further increased, taking into consideration the social services which the Post Office provides through the circulation of all types of mail. I do not think we can sum it all up with a few references to dollar losses or gains; the postal service is much greater than that, in my opinion.
The second area in which the Post Office is losing money relates to the imbalance of what it must carry
24081-18i

March 29, 1971
Government Organization Act, 1970 free of charge, largely emanating from the United States. As hon. members know, the universal postal agreement is basically a simple understanding between countries that they will carry the mail of another free of charge. This is an excellent basis for co-operation around the world and 132 countries are now involved on this basis. But Canada finds herself in a unique position with respect to the United States, a country with ten times its population. Canada is naturally required in these circumstances to carry a much greater volume of mail from the United States free of charge than is the United States with respect to Canadian mail. The imbalance of foreign mail, largely from the United States, leads to a loss in the order of $5 million every year. Efforts should be continued-and I know that some are being made-to rectify this situation.
A third area in which we need to improve the situation of the Post Office involves our quaint procedure of giving free accommodation to post offices and then requiring the Post Office to service departments of government free. This is an outmoded way of doing business and we should change it. We heard from the Post Office last week some good news for a change. Instead of being told about impending increases in postal rates or reductions in the service or disputes with employees, we were told about a new and more efficient method of handling mail, a new zip code procedure, probably the best type in the world, which would speed mail deliveries. This is a good step forward.
It seems to me sometimes that in the postal service, as in other spheres of endeavour, we suffer from the fact that while we are actually living in conditions of the future, we are still mired in the old ideas of the past. Electronics, which no doubt will play an increasingly important role in the postal services, will in future make it unnecessary, for example, to mail millions of old age pension cheques or family allowance cheques, largely to the same recipients, every few weeks or so. It will be possible to have this money deposited regularly in the accounts of recipients across Canada by electronic impulses, thus eliminating the need to mail and deliver millions of these bits of paper.
In conclusion, I wish to make these recommendations. We have heard that the Post Office is contemplating an increase in first and second-class mail rates. My recommendation is that there should be no increase in the first-class mail rate. It is not very long since we increased the charge on local mail by 50 per cent and by 20 per cent in the case of on-going mail. First-class mail over the years has come very close to paying its own way and it is still in that area: out of the five cents per capita per week which I mentioned as being the cost to Canadians of the postal deficit, the loss on first-class mail amounts to between half a cent and one cent a week.
! Then again, the largest part of the first-class mail no longer consists of letters written by individuals to other individuals. The great bulk of it is sent out by business firms in the form of bills-hydro bills, telephone bills, oil and gas bills, and so on-to consumers. My contention is that if the first-class mail rate is again increased, these

corporations will find that their costs have been increased and will soon pass the increase back to the people who receive the bills. In effect, we may find that the ordinary letter-writers of Canada are paying twice- they will pay more when they buy stamps because the price will have gone up, and they will be charged more for their telephone or hydro bills because those bills will cost more to deliver. I say, please leave the first-class mail rate as it is.
In the second place, I think it would be wise if we were to take a hard look at the profit-oriented mail in Canada. This is the area in which we are losing about half of this five cent per capita loss per week. If we have to increase this rate further, let us do so, although we must keep in mind the services in employment, the creation of business and extent of the communications which come within the realm of second-class mail. It is not a matter of saying that we are losing "X" dollars on second-class mail and have to increase the rate. We have to think beyond that and take a comprehensive look at it. I think the loss on second-class mail is about 2J cents, at the most three cents, per capita per week.
Thirdly, let us press on to gain an adjustment of the imbalance of what it costs Canada to carry foreign mail under the international postal agreement. I think we can hope to reduce the approximately $5 million which that imbalance presently costs Canadians. Finally, I think we should realize that with all its difficulties and troubles, our postal service is a very excellent one and has set a very good example to private organizations in Canada. When you consider the millions of people it serves without error, the little cost to the community involved and the fact that it is part of a world wide organization-132 countries participate in the international postal service-I feel that our Post Office is a worthy one and that we should consider how best to improve it in regard both to its efficiency and the reduction of its costs.

I know that the minister who is to be in charge of the Post Office is a man of modern ideas and good will. I know that he would be the last man to accept certain suggestions and would not willingly be forced into a position in which he would need to repudiate the futuristic and 99 per cent nonsensical suggestions of his predecessor. I do not want to delve into or touch upon that particularly sensitive area.
I have spent some time in this House discussing the kind of extravaganzas the Minister of Communications has embarked upon. At times he seemed to believe that the transportation and communication of the written word was totally passe and that we should be thinking of the futuristic conveyance of ideas. Where the hardware

that was to transport these ideas was to come from was something which could be left for future generations to decide I suspect that the Post Office bothered and bored him. As I walked to the House of Commons at two o'clock this afternoon, I saw the Lapalme drivers. These are men who have come down day after day in good weather and bad weather. I thought perhaps he was adopting a protective colouration and the kind of psychological evacuation that all mortal men are inclined to follow, because I suspect he was not thinking very much of the Post Office. I suspected that he might look the other way when he saw these Lapalme workers, and that he might be thinking of Tele-sat and other devices for communication which were not so mundane, so dreary or so common as to involve something as simple as the delivering of mail from a remote child to its father or mother. With such devices, he would not be bothered about the delivery of a statement from a business house to one of its customers, or the delivery of a statement from the customer to the business house: he would not be bothered too much about church papers, about academic journals or about those media of thoughtful, intellectual communication which pleaded with the minister and which for months told him about the problems that would be created if he failed to relent. He was told of the strict, stringent, hurtful, unnecessary and improper inhibitions which would be placed upon the communication of ideas in a time and in a country in which the free market and movement of ideas was more important than ever before.
I can remember so well, Mr. Chairman, when the Minister of Communications, an eminent businessman far more successful in that field than I, an impecunious ex-professor could ever be, told us how he was going to assault and assail these iniquitous deficits in the Post Office and how he ranged back over the years, talking of the carelessness of his predecessors-I am afraid that I must include the minister-designate in this category-and how he condemned what he called wastefulness and lack of business capacity. However, there is a question which bothers me which I believe I should put to the President of the Treasury Board since he is the pilot of this legislation.
I do not know of any other full minister in the cabinet who has attached to the legislation which establishes his status a proviso-a Damoclesian sword-under which he can lose that position. For example, in this bill there is to be established a minister of the environment and he is to be the minister of the environment-period. By clause 26 now before us we provide that there shall be a Postmaster General, but we keep alive in subclause 3 the provision that if the Prime Minister does not name anyone as Postmaster General, the Minister of Communications gets the job again. It would be a fate worse than being buried to have him back again. However, as long as he stays on this side of the House we are probably safe. Frankly, I think the President of the Treasury Board was reaching a fair distance for the reasons for which subclause 3 of clause 26 reads. I think this is really a case of sloppy drafting, or an attempt by the government to preserve some kind of pecking order within its own ranks. Either we are to have a separate minister in charge of the Post Office, or we are not.
The Prime Minister may at any time choose to have a person in charge of each ministry, or he may choose to double up ministers and have one person in charge of two or three departments. There does not need to be any legislation. The feasibility of setting up a Crown corporation instead of a Post Office Department is something that is yet to be heard about in a formal manner in the House; and, as my colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said, that would require legislation. If at that time the government of the day wanted to set up such a Crown corporation, they would put a provision in the legislation which would do away with a separate minister of the Crown in charge of the Post Office. I think that essentially the clause is sloppily drafted, or it might be due to an oversight on the part of the drafters or the President of the Treasury Board.
Therefore, I would like to move an amendment to clause 26 as follows:
That clause 26 be amended by deleting the words "Subject to subsection 3" from line 16, and by deleting the lines 22 to 29 on page 8.
This would clean up the clause and eliminate what I think is superfluous wording in the bill.

maintopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-INCENTIVE GRANTS- ACQUISITION OF PROPORTIONATE EQUITY IN RECIPIENT COMPANIES
REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-INCENTIVE GRANTS- ACQUISITION OF PROPORTIONATE EQUITY IN RECIPIENT COMPANIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I could not help but notice your impatience with the delay in proceeding with the adjournment debate tonight. I can only take it that you must be anxious to hear the hon. member for Fraser Valley West. For that reason, I should like now to take part in this debate because I think there is something basically wrong and inequitable in the way the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marc-hand) makes awards of public money under the Industrial incentives act. As I see it, what is basically wrong is that the priorities of industry rather than those of gov-

ernment initiate the series of procedures which culminate in a plant or industry locating in community "X" rather than in community "Y". We in Canada have some serious regional economic problems, and the Industrial incentives act was established to deal with them.
What was in my opinion originally envisioned as a palliative to employment in slow-growth areas should receive commendation from all quarters of this House. My intervention tonight does not deal with the principle of government stimulation to areas in need, but instead with the practicalities of how these grants are administered. As I said, it is a private corporation rather than the government of Canada which through its application of grants to industrialists-which are described by some as social welfare-provides the initiative. Little or no concern has been directed to the planning or recognition of our own national priorities.
What, for instance, does the department do about relating a particular industry to a particular area, its suitability, etc? On the contrary, it is up to the industry to make application initially. It then follows that a particular industry rather than the national government establishes whether or not a plant locates in a particular community. The celebrated economist and former Canadian, John Kenneth Galbraith, has made the point that large multicorporations have little difficulty in raising capital. They do it largely through retained earnings. What, I ask, is the rationale behind the recent awards which I will list: $1.1 million to Boeing of Canada, $6 million to that poor company from the United States called IBM, $1 million to Ashland Chemicals, and $4 million to Control Data of Canada? These are a few examples of recent grants to foreign corporations operated in our country for which, aside from the jobs produced, Canada as a nation may gain relatively little.
This prompted me to direct the following question to the Minister on February 25, as recorded at page 3740 of Hansard.
In awarding these various incentive grants amounting sometimes to millions of dollars and ranging in value from $3,000 to $5,000 per job, has the government considered acquiring equity in the recipient company proportionately equivalent to the grant made?
Your Honour suggested that this was a representation. I then said:
It seems to me that there is a basic inequity in the fact that when a recipient company makes a profit its shareholders get the benefit, but if it loses the public picks up the tab.
I asked this question for the following reasons, Mr. Speaker. First, it appears that we have put through incentive grants which total in excess of $100 million and this vast amount of money could have been used to acquire Canadian equity in certain companies, especially the foreign ones, and a greater control of our own economy-a crucial matter presently under study by the cabinet. Second, I was alarmed that grants tended to vary from region to region. This indicated no real planning at the decision-making or ministerial level. For example, Nova Scotia received $15,000 per job, Newfoundland
March 29, 1971

$1,600 per job, roughly 10 per cent of Nova Scotia's, and Ontario $7,000 per job. The Canadian average is $5,500 per job.
Certain provinces, notably Manitoba and the reactionary Saskatchewan government, have seen fit to tie equity into their incentive grants. For the proposed Meadow Lake pulp mill the government of Saskatchewan has assured 30 per cent equity as its price for its share of assistance. Surely for the $12 million requested, the government of Canada ought to consider eight per cent to 10 per cent equity as a fair proportion if the project is ultimately approved by the minister. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, the New Democratic Party envisions the Canada Development Corporation as a Crown corporation which with the involvement of the provincial and municipal governments and co-operatives could be a means whereby a substantially larger proportion of Canada's industry and resource development could be retained in Canadian hands.
I know that a substantial portion of the minister's rebuttal will centre around the argument that industries are granted public funds as an incentive to locate away from the comparative cost advantage areas in large metropolitan regions. This argument I repudiate.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there are many aspects of the hon. member's remarks this evening with which one could take issue. Under the terms of the Regional Development Incentives Act it would be impossible for the government to acquire equity in projects which it supports. maintopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-INCENTIVE GRANTS- ACQUISITION OF PROPORTIONATE EQUITY IN RECIPIENT COMPANIES

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
maintopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-INCENTIVE GRANTS- ACQUISITION OF PROPORTIONATE EQUITY IN RECIPIENT COMPANIES
speechtext:
The program is designed to create new jobs in those parts of the country where they are most badly needed. To do this, it must offer a real incentive to industries to locate or expand in areas where they might not otherwise do so. The program therefore works by providing manufacturing industries with grants sufficiently large in relation to their costs-this is why there is a variation-to enable them to undertake viable projects despite the difficulties they may encounter as a result of location in a slow-growth region. If the govern-
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion ment were to acquire equity in return for its grants, the present incentive in favour of the slow-growth regions would disappear.

maintopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-INCENTIVE GRANTS- ACQUISITION OF PROPORTIONATE EQUITY IN RECIPIENT COMPANIES
speechtext: Oh, come on!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
maintopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-INCENTIVE GRANTS- ACQUISITION OF PROPORTIONATE EQUITY IN RECIPIENT COMPANIES
speechtext:
Think about it for a moment. The government would simply become another source of equity financing, that is, in return for the grant it would acquire an equity in the company. There would be no incentive left. While there is perhaps a case to be made for the government taking equity in certain circumstances, it would have to be in addition to the assistance available under the existing incentives program rather than a replacement for it. This is a possibility which has been considered within the department although no action has been taken in that direction.
I would refer to the hon. member to the statement made today by the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) before the Standing Committee on Economic Development. In this statement he referred to at least two new federal-provincial industrial development corporations which will operate in Newfoundland and New Brunswick and which, among other things, may supply equity capital in certain circumstances.

AIR TRANSPORT-USE OF AIR SPACE AND AIRPORTS BY SUPERSONIC PLANES-AWARENESS OF OTHER COUNTRIES OF CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it always happens that when my hon. friend, my seatmate, appears on the late night show he insists that I appear along with him. We have to keep each other company.
On March 23 I directed a question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) with regard to the use of Canadian air space by supersonic planes. I asked him whether other countries were aware of the position taken by Canada. The minister replied that he had certainly made our position known to the United States, for example, but he did not know whether this information had been formally conveyed to other countries which might be concerned. He had not done so personally. I then asked the following supplementary question:
Would the minister say whether he would formally convey that expression of opinion, which I heartily support, to the other countries of the world now engaged in supersonic aircraft programs?
At that point, Mr. Speaker, you suggested that my supplementary was, in fact, a representation.

maintopic: AIR TRANSPORT-USE OF AIR SPACE AND AIRPORTS BY SUPERSONIC PLANES-AWARENESS OF OTHER COUNTRIES OF CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext: He was right.

maintopic: AIR TRANSPORT-USE OF AIR SPACE AND AIRPORTS BY SUPERSONIC PLANES-AWARENESS OF OTHER COUNTRIES OF CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext: Yes, it was.

maintopic: AIR TRANSPORT-USE OF AIR SPACE AND AIRPORTS BY SUPERSONIC PLANES-AWARENESS OF OTHER COUNTRIES OF CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext:
At this point I think it is important we face the question whether or not our stand with regard

March 29, 1971
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
to supersonic transport is appreciated by the other countries which are involved in this experiment. All of us are aware that the United States Senate and House of Representatives have turned down requests for funds to continue the supersonic aircraft program in that country. This decision has resulted in repercussions not only in the United States but throughout the world.
All the unanswered questions regarding the effects of using supersonic aircraft are now being asked again, and I am sure that those who are concerned with the building of the "Concorde" in France and Britain are questioning whether or not the program should be carried on. Here in Canada we ought also to ask certain questions about these supersonic planes which travel between 1,400 and 1,800 miles an hour, cost between $40 million and $50 million each and create a disastrous sonic boom which could injure people and property lying under their path. Do these planes, flying at great height, produce exhaust gases which by polluting the upper atmosphere could give rise to real danger? At the same time we must realize that those people with the technical know-how to build this sort of plane are not concerned with the environmental pollution they create or whether people's brains will be damaged by resultant sonic booms.
The question that the government must answer is whether SST's are to be allowed to fly over Canadian soil and to use Canadian airports. People and planners say that airports must be built away from urban centres so that sonic booms will not wreck our brains. But how do these supersonic planes reach our airports? I am sure that the people who say we must build airports a long way from large urban centres also appreciate that rural communities are just as concerned about some booms as anybody else. It is clear from two answers that were tabled that Air Canada has on order at the present time ten supersonic jet aircraft. For the "Concorde" SST there are four line positions which call for delivery in approximately 1976. There are six line positions for the Boeing 2707 calling for delivery in the spring of 1980.
I asked the following questions of the minister: Have the Department of Transport or the Canadian Transport Commission approved of supersonic planes flying over and landing in Canada? The answer was no. Then I asked: What specific research has been undertaken by any government agency or department regarding the effects of supersonic flying over Canada? The department replied there was none, that the Department is following the development of this type of aircraft from the viewpoint of applying restrictive measures should this action appear necessary. Another question I asked was: Is the Canadian Transport Commission or the Department of Transport aware of the recent announcement by Air Canada that six Boeing supersonic planes have been ordered to be flying in Canada around 1978? The answer was yes. Then I asked: Has approval been given to the flying of the above planes over Canada? The answer was no.
There is much talk in this House of protecting the environment, of national pollution standards and clean air standards. All these aspects must also involve use of

supersonic jets. I am sure we all realize that our nationalized airline has now on order a supersonic aircraft that has not been given permission to fly over our territory or to land at our airports. If the Minister of Transport wants to be a great statesman, all he has to do is introduce legislation to prohibit the landing of these planes at any of our airports and to prohibit SSTs flying over our territory. I am sure in this regard Canada could lead the way for other countries involved in the race for SSTs by introducing this type of legislation.
It is hard to imagine why the Canadian Transport Commission or the Air Transport Board of the commission has not done some research in this area. I am sure that if the people of Canada had their way they would not allow the SSTs, in which billions of dollars have been invested, to fly over our land and to land at our airports when they have no knowledge of the disastrous effects that could result from such flights.
